messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Sounds like you are headed toward a spatial model, and that it will morph into a spatial hurdle model. For both those reasons, you probably want to keep working with estimation and prediction stacks, like Finn says, and also think about how to code this in inlabru as the predict() function makes predictions a lot more automagic. But, just in case you want some quick info on generating predictions using a simple inla model like the one you are starting with, here is some code to get you started.

# libraries
library(dplyr); library(ggplot2); library(INLA); library(inlabru)

# sample size
n.gear <- 2; n.hab <- 3; n.sample <- 30; n <- n.gear * n.sample

# factor levels
gear <- gl(n = n.gear, k = n.sample, length = n)
habitat <- gl(n = n.hab, k = n.sample / n.hab, length = n)

# effects
baseline <- 40    # intercept
gear.effects <- -10 # gear effect
habitat.effects <- c(5, 10)    # habitat effects
all.effects <- c(baseline, gear.effects, habitat.effects)

# error
sigma <- 3
eps <- rnorm(n, 0, sigma)

# model matrix
X <- as.matrix(model.matrix(~ gear+habitat) ); X

# response
pos <- as.numeric(as.matrix(X) %*% as.matrix(all.effects) + eps)

# all data in a dataframe
d1 <- data.frame(pos=pos, intercept=1) %>%
  bind_cols(as.data.frame(X) %>% select(-1)) %>%
  mutate(gear=gear, habitat=habitat)

# plot it
d1 %>%
  ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=habitat, y=pos)) + facet_wrap(~gear)

# add some prediction rows to the input data just to show how it works
d2 <- d1 %>% mutate(pos=NA) %>% distinct()
d1 <- d1 %>% rbind(d2)

# inla model
in1 <- inla(pos ~ gear + habitat,
           data=d1,
           control.compute=list(config=T),
           control.predict=list(compute=T))
summary(in1)

# get inla posterior sample
s1 <- inla.posterior.sample(100, in1)
row.names(s1[[1]]$latent)

# pull out samples for the prediction rows 61-66
pred_samps <- t(inla.posterior.sample.eval("Predictor", s1)[61:66,])
head(pred_samps)

# pull out samples for the effects. then you can do any
# kind of prediction you want using the linear predictor
all_samps <- data.frame(
  int_samps=as.numeric(inla.posterior.sample.eval("(Intercept)", s1)),
  gear2_samps=as.numeric(inla.posterior.sample.eval("gear2", s1)),
  habitat2_samps=as.numeric(inla.posterior.sample.eval("habitat2", s1)),
  habitat3_samps=as.numeric(inla.posterior.sample.eval("habitat3", s1)))
head(all_samps)

# or use an inlabru model
br1 <- bru(pos ~ gear2 + habitat2 + habitat3,
            data=d1)
summary(br1)

# and get inlabru predictions
d1 %>%
  select(gear2) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  predict(object = br1, formula = ~ gear2)
d1 %>%
  select(habitat2, habitat3) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  predict(object = br1, formula = ~ habitat2 + habitat3)

messages.body_plain:
You need to think of the model as something that exists regardless of whether it’s being observed or not. In the setup you describe, you’ll get predictions for the inputs you specify with NA responses.

Finn

> On 17 Aug 2022, at 01:04, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿No, I was speaking about what the practical effect is when there’s a lack of observations. If the specified model is identifiable based on the provided observations, it will estimate it according to the resulting posterior distribution (unless it results in numerical or memory problems).

>
>
> Finn
>
> > On 16 Aug 2022, at 22:54, Kyle Manning <manning...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > ﻿The model is an AR model replicated iid across individuals.
> >
> > So, an AR(3) will exclude individuals with less than 3 observations from the fitting process?
> > I guess that makes sense.
> >
> > I'm still not quite understanding how the "prediction/reconstruction" works.
> >
> > For example, if the data setup is:
> >
> > individual |  sample  |  response
> > 1               |         1       | ...
> > 1               |         2       |
> > 1               |         3       |
> > ...
> > 1               |         20     |
> > 2               |         1       |

> > 3               |         1       |
> >
> > But, I also have a set I want predictions on
> >

> > 2               |         3         |       NA
> > 3               |         2         |       NA
> >
> > How does this work for individuals 2 and 3?
> >
> > Will predictions for individual 2 use the AR model with samples 1 & 2, and similarly will only sample 1 be used for individual 3?
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, August 16, 2022 at 3:40:46 PM UTC-5 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Can you clarify more precisely how you’re defining the model?

messages.body_plain:
Hi, that depends a bit on the type of random effect, and whether it’s for an observed point or an unobserved point.
For iid effects and observed points, the estimated random effect value is included in the model, so no special trick is needed.
For iid effects for new point, I.e. actual prediction/extrapolation/interpolation, you can sample from it using the sampled value of the precision parameter. You’ll need to look in the sampling output to find the name of the specific parameter.
For spde effects, no special handling is needed, as the whole defined domain is part of the model.
For other structured random effects, the only simple way is to make sure that all locations you want to predict for are part of the estimated model (which is what using a “prediction stack” can be used for).

Finn

> For spde effects, no special handling is needed, as the whole defined domain is part of the model.

But something you might not know if you are new to INLA, you can always add rows to your dataset with NA for the response variable and INLA will fill in predicted values with summaries. So you can specify whatever combinations of the gear and habitat variables you want, put in an NA for the response, add those rows to the data, and extract the predictions from the results object. messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much for your responses.

At the base of my question was a lack of understanding how an AR effect is incorporated in the Bayesian predictive setting.

I am still hung up on some seemingly untrustworthy results I get from fitting an AR model.
For observations where individuals haven't been observed before, the fitted values are much, much too close to the true response.

Do you have any idea why this might happen?

Kyle

On Tuesday, August 16, 2022 at 7:06:28 PM UTC-5 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> You need to think of the model as something that exists regardless of whether it’s being observed or not. In the setup you describe, you’ll get predictions for the inputs you specify with NA responses.
>
> Finn
>
> > On 17 Aug 2022, at 01:04, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > ﻿No, I was speaking about what the practical effect is when there’s a lack of observations. If the specified model is identifiable based on the provided observations, it will estimate it according to the resulting posterior distribution (unless it results in numerical or memory problems).
> >
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > > On 16 Aug 2022, at 22:54, Kyle Manning <manning...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > ﻿The model is an AR model replicated iid across individuals.
> > >
> > > So, an AR(3) will exclude individuals with less than 3 observations from the fitting process?
> > > I guess that makes sense.
> > >
> > > I'm still not quite understanding how the "prediction/reconstruction" works.
> > >
> > > For example, if the data setup is:
> > >
> > > individual |  sample  |  response
> > > 1               |         1       | ...
> > > 1               |         2       |
> > > 1               |         3       |
> > > ...
> > > 1               |         20     |
> > > 2               |         1       |
> > > 2               |         2       |
> > > 3               |         1       |
> > >
> > > But, I also have a set I want predictions on
> > >
> > > individual |  sample  |  response
> > > 1               |         21       |       NA
> > > 2               |         3         |       NA
> > > 3               |         2         |       NA
> > >
> > > How does this work for individuals 2 and 3?
> > >
> > > Will predictions for individual 2 use the AR model with samples 1 & 2, and similarly will only sample 1 be used for individual 3?
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, August 16, 2022 at 3:40:46 PM UTC-5 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Can you clarify more precisely how you’re defining the model?
> > > > If it’s a joint AR model for all individuals, you’ll simply have more information for time point with more observations.
> > > > If it’s and AR model that’s replicated iid across individuals, then it will rely on there being enough individuals with information about the ar parameters; if it’s able to estimate the ar parameters with only those individuals included, then it should in principle handle having the sparsely observed individuals as well; it will in effect do prediction/reconstruction for all unobserved time points.
> > > >
> > > > Finn
> > > >
> > > > > On 16 Aug 2022, at 21:17, Kyle Manning <manning...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > ﻿Hello all,
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm fitting an AR(p) model on unbalanced panel data, where some individuals may be observed only once and some have up to 20 observations.
> > > > >
> > > > > My question is: when using AR models in INLA, I am curious how having different # of observations for individuals is handled - if I fit an AR(3) model and yet many individuals have only 1 observation, what happens/ how is this handled internally?
> > > > >
> > > > > Thank you,
> > > > > Kyle

example, with person.1 being observed at time 1,2,4,4, (yes, twice at
time 4),and person.2 being observed at time 2,3,5, then

idx=c(1,2,4,4,2,3,5)
r=c(1,1,1,1,2,2,2)
values=1:5

and you use

	f(idx, model="ar1", replicate=r, values=values)

its important to give 'values' which are 1:n for which n is the max time
for the AR1 to be observed or you want it to exists.

to experiment with this, you can fix the observational noise with

family="gaussian",
control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(PREC),
fixed=TRUE))))

where PREC=1/VAR, like exp(14) if you have 'exact' observations.

with few observations it can be a little tricky to balance noise
observations and the properties of the AR1, as you have multiple
interpretations of the data.

messages.subject: Posterior eval error when using experimental mode
messages.subject_clean: Posterior eval error when using experimental mode
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I am attempting to fit a binomial model on survey data and then generate samples from the posterior using inla.posterior.sample() and inla.posterior.sample.eval().

Due to the data set I am using being large, I can only fit the model when I use inla.mode = 'experimental' instead of inla.mode = 'classic'. This seems to cause an issue when I get down to using the inla.posterior.sample.eval() function as the model fit using inla.mode = 'experimental' returns the following error "Error in a.sample$latent[.contents$start[i]:(.contents$start[i] + .contents$length[i] -  : subscript out of bounds" whereas the model fit using inla.mode = 'classic' does not return this error.

To highlight this, below I have included an example of the code I am running with some fake data. Any variables labelled with 1 (e.g., fit1, samp1, eval1a) are relating to the model fit using inla.mode = 'experimental' and any variables labelled with 2 are relating to the model fit using inla.model = 'classic'. The aforementioned error is returned when I attempt to run eval1a but not eval2a.

Looking at the error, it says there are issues relating to subscript in the latent part of the sample where the subscript is found from the model contents. Both model contents (fit1$misc$configs$contents and fit2$misc$configs$contents) are exactly the same and when looking at the latent sample, the only difference was the experimental mode labels the latent column V1 rather than sample:1 like the classic mode. I changed this to see if it did anything but unfortnely the error still persisted and I am at a bit of a loss as what to do now...

If anyone has any advice as how to run inla.mode = 'experimental' with inla.posterior.sample.eval(), it would be greatly appreciated!

Thank you,
Connor

P.s. Also, on a really quick second note... at the bottom eval1c and eval2c are more similar to what I am doing with the actual data. For the function 'my.fun' used within eval1c and eval2c, is this the correct way to handle factors and random effects that are put into the model?

###############################################################

# packages ----

library(tidyverse)
library(INLA)

# data ----

# setting the seed
set.seed(1234)

# length of data
n = 100

dat <-
  data.frame(
    # random id
    id = 1:n,
    # age: continuous, adults between 16 and 100
    age = sample(16:100, n, replace = TRUE),
    # sex: factor 1 for male and 2 for female
    sex = sample(1:2, n, replace = TRUE) %>% factor(., levels = 1:2),
    # marital status: factor 1-9 for different classifications
    marStat = sample(1:9, n, replace = TRUE) %>% factor(., levels = 1:9),
    # observed outcome: binary 0 or 1
    y = sample(0:1, n, replace = TRUE))

# formula ----

formula <- y ~ 1 + age + sex + marStat + f(id, model = 'iid')

# model fit ----

verbose = TRUE

## using inla.mode = 'experimental' ----

fit1<-
  INLA::inla(formula,
             family = 'binomial',
             data = dat,
             control.compute = list(config = TRUE),
             control.predictor = list(compute = FALSE, link = 1),
             control.inla = list(strategy = 'adaptive', int.strategy = 'auto'),
             inla.mode = 'experimental',
             lincomb = NULL,
             verbose = verbose)

## using inla.mode = 'classic' ----

fit2<-
  INLA::inla(formula,
             family = 'binomial',
             data = dat,
             control.compute = list(config = TRUE),
             control.predictor = list(compute = FALSE, link = 1),
             control.inla = list(strategy = 'adaptive', int.strategy = 'auto'),
             inla.mode = 'classic',
             lincomb = NULL,
             verbose = verbose)

# prediction ----

## number of samples ----

nsim = 100

## stop predictor being sampled for compuational reasons ----

# contents tags

messages.body_plain:
The AR model is defined to be stationary, i.e. at time 1 it has the
stationary distribution, so it's not "free". The inla.doc("ar") ar.pdf
documentation says "the joint distribution for {xt , t = 1, . . . ,
p}, is
set to the stationary distribution for the process, hence there are no
boundary issues".

Also, when you have an ar model with replicates, the time points are
the same for all individuals, i.e. you need
  values=seq_len(maximum_time_lag)
to ensure all time points are included, like Haavard stated.

(To have different time intervals for different individuals, you would
need to build a bespoke model with "rgeneric". If the time intervals
are similar in length, it's much easier to use the built-in
"replicated ar" approach.)

What is the setting under which you "train" and "test"? Under a model
where the AR model is directly observed, plus measurement noise,
predictions for new individuals would have variance s^2 (where s is
the estimated AR model standard deviation) whereas predictions for
observed time points of an individual in the training set would have
variance
around 1/(1/s^2+1/s_obs^2), where s_obs is the observation standard
deviation, which is smaller than both s^2 and s_obs^2. For temporal
interpolation the variance will be somewhere between those two
prediction variances.
It's not clear to me what type of "overfitting" you are referring to?

Finn

messages.body_plain:
And the corresponding sd values? If the observation noise variance is estimated to be small, then the AR estimates will pass vary close to the observed values with small posterior sd. That in itself isn’t overfitting; e.g. one could have a model where the ar process is directly observed at the observation times. This is only a problem if it’s a problem in the specific context.

Finn

> To perform my training and testing I create a second target column, 'target2', and set a sample of the values to be NA. Then I call inla(target2 ~ f(timesteps, model='ar', order=1, replicate=id_f, values=1:max(df$timesteps), constr=FALSE + ...).
>

>
> Something is causing the model to fit far too well to some of the individuals' first observations
>
> On Thursday, August 18, 2022 at 8:50:06 AM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:

> > stationary distribution, so it's not "free". The inla.doc("ar") ar.pdf
> > documentation says "the joint distribution for {xt , t = 1, . . . ,
> > p}, is
> > set to the stationary distribution for the process, hence there are no
> > boundary issues".
> >

> > the same for all individuals, i.e. you need
> > values=seq_len(maximum_time_lag)
> > to ensure all time points are included, like Haavard stated.
> >
> > (To have different time intervals for different individuals, you would
> > need to build a bespoke model with "rgeneric". If the time intervals
> > are similar in length, it's much easier to use the built-in
> > "replicated ar" approach.)
> >
> > What is the setting under which you "train" and "test"? Under a model
> > where the AR model is directly observed, plus measurement noise,
> > predictions for new individuals would have variance s^2 (where s is
> > the estimated AR model standard deviation) whereas predictions for
> > observed time points of an individual in the training set would have
> > variance
> > around 1/(1/s^2+1/s_obs^2), where s_obs is the observation standard
> > deviation, which is smaller than both s^2 and s_obs^2. For temporal
> > interpolation the variance will be somewhere between those two
> > prediction variances.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] AR terms for unbalanced panel data
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] AR terms for unbalanced panel data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

this is more a question of what the Baeysian methodology does rather
than any particular thing about how INLA does prediction; it just does
the best it can at computing information about the posterior
distributions for the specified model.

It doesn't reconstruct a "0th" observation. It just reconstructs all
the latent variables of the defined model.
Consider the case when the specified model has iid replicates of a
time-stationary  AR(1) process model, and the observation model is
additive Gaussian noise, and the only other model component is an
intercept.
Let the AR(1) variables be x_{t,j}, for time t and individual j, with
variance \sigma_x^2 and AR correlation parameter \rho.

Then for observation i, the linear predictor evaluates that for some
time t_i and individual j_i:
  \eta_i = x_{t_i,j_i} + \beta_0
The observed values are
  y_i = \eta_i + \eps_i,
where \eps_i ~ N(0,\sigma_e^2).

The *.fitted.values output contains the posterior distribution
information for the \eta_i values. (i.e. the sum of \beta_0 and
x-values for observed times&individuals)
The *.random output contains the posterior distribution information
for the x_{t,j} values.

The x-variables exist regardless of the observations. The f()
mechanism allows us to construct models where x_{t,j} is defined on
the full grid of all combinations of t=1,...,T and j=1,...,J,
and the summary.random output will contain the posterior distribution
information for all of those variables, regardless of whether some or
all have been observed.
If you plot the posterior std.dev <http://std.dev> values for all t=1,...,T for a
single individual, you should see small values for times associated
with observations, and progressively larger values for further,
unobserved, time points.
If the covariance parameters were known and fixed, the variances for
observed time points would be on the order of
  1 / (1 / \sigma_x^2 + 1 / \sigma_e^2)
(not exactly that, but as a rough guide) and then increasing towards
\sigma_x^2 the further from the observed time points you get.
For an individual that hasn't been observed at all,

For cases where for some individuals you only have observations for
the first few time indices, this is more computationally costly than
if you build a bespoke model that allows different max-T for each j
(you can do this with rgeneric). However, the cost of AR(1)
computations is only of order linear in T, so whether it's worth the
extra implementation effort depends on how "imbalanced" your T-values
are.

I'm not sure if this answers your question...

Finn

Thanks Finn, that does help explain a lot. So in $summary.random I have all of the distributions for my X_t,j and the model constructs X_t,j even when time timestep t does not exist for individual j. But these won't be present in the *.fitted.values since there isn't actually an observation for them.

On Friday, August 19, 2022 at 9:08:57 AM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi,
>
> this is more a question of what the Baeysian methodology does rather
> than any particular thing about how INLA does prediction; it just does
> the best it can at computing information about the posterior
> distributions for the specified model.
>
> It doesn't reconstruct a "0th" observation. It just reconstructs all
> the latent variables of the defined model.
> Consider the case when the specified model has iid replicates of a
> time-stationary AR(1) process model, and the observation model is
> additive Gaussian noise, and the only other model component is an
> intercept.
> Let the AR(1) variables be x_{t,j}, for time t and individual j, with
> variance \sigma_x^2 and AR correlation parameter \rho.
>
> Then for observation i, the linear predictor evaluates that for some
> time t_i and individual j_i:
> \eta_i = x_{t_i,j_i} + \beta_0
> The observed values are
> y_i = \eta_i + \eps_i,
> where \eps_i ~ N(0,\sigma_e^2).
>
> The *.fitted.values output contains the posterior distribution
> information for the \eta_i values. (i.e. the sum of \beta_0 and
> x-values for observed times&individuals)
> The *.random output contains the posterior distribution information
> for the x_{t,j} values.
>
> The x-variables exist regardless of the observations. The f()
> mechanism allows us to construct models where x_{t,j} is defined on
> the full grid of all combinations of t=1,...,T and j=1,...,J,
> and the summary.random output will contain the posterior distribution
> information for all of those variables, regardless of whether some or
> all have been observed.
> If you plot the posterior std.dev <http://std.dev> values for all t=1,...,T for a
> single individual, you should see small values for times associated
> with observations, and progressively larger values for further,
> unobserved, time points.
> If the covariance parameters were known and fixed, the variances for
> observed time points would be on the order of
> 1 / (1 / \sigma_x^2 + 1 / \sigma_e^2)
> (not exactly that, but as a rough guide) and then increasing towards
> \sigma_x^2 the further from the observed time points you get.
> For an individual that hasn't been observed at all,
>
> For cases where for some individuals you only have observations for
> the first few time indices, this is more computationally costly than
> if you build a bespoke model that allows different max-T for each j
> (you can do this with rgeneric). However, the cost of AR(1)
> computations is only of order linear in T, so whether it's worth the
> extra implementation effort depends on how "imbalanced" your T-values
> are.
>
> I'm not sure if this answers your question...
>
> Finn
>

> > >
> > > On Friday, August 19, 2022 at 9:08:57 AM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Hi,
> > > >
> > > > this is more a question of what the Baeysian methodology does rather
> > > > than any particular thing about how INLA does prediction; it just does
> > > > the best it can at computing information about the posterior
> > > > distributions for the specified model.
> > > >
> > > > It doesn't reconstruct a "0th" observation. It just reconstructs all
> > > > the latent variables of the defined model.
> > > > Consider the case when the specified model has iid replicates of a
> > > > time-stationary AR(1) process model, and the observation model is
> > > > additive Gaussian noise, and the only other model component is an
> > > > intercept.
> > > > Let the AR(1) variables be x_{t,j}, for time t and individual j, with
> > > > variance \sigma_x^2 and AR correlation parameter \rho.
> > > >
> > > > Then for observation i, the linear predictor evaluates that for some
> > > > time t_i and individual j_i:
> > > > \eta_i = x_{t_i,j_i} + \beta_0
> > > > The observed values are
> > > > y_i = \eta_i + \eps_i,
> > > > where \eps_i ~ N(0,\sigma_e^2).
> > > >
> > > > The *.fitted.values output contains the posterior distribution
> > > > information for the \eta_i values. (i.e. the sum of \beta_0 and
> > > > x-values for observed times&individuals)
> > > > The *.random output contains the posterior distribution information
> > > > for the x_{t,j} values.
> > > >
> > > > The x-variables exist regardless of the observations. The f()
> > > > mechanism allows us to construct models where x_{t,j} is defined on
> > > > the full grid of all combinations of t=1,...,T and j=1,...,J,
> > > > and the summary.random output will contain the posterior distribution
> > > > information for all of those variables, regardless of whether some or
> > > > all have been observed.
> > > > If you plot the posterior std.dev <http://std.dev> values for all t=1,...,T for a
> > > > single individual, you should see small values for times associated
> > > > with observations, and progressively larger values for further,
> > > > unobserved, time points.
> > > > If the covariance parameters were known and fixed, the variances for
> > > > observed time points would be on the order of
> > > > 1 / (1 / \sigma_x^2 + 1 / \sigma_e^2)
> > > > (not exactly that, but as a rough guide) and then increasing towards
> > > > \sigma_x^2 the further from the observed time points you get.
> > > > For an individual that hasn't been observed at all,
> > > >
> > > > For cases where for some individuals you only have observations for
> > > > the first few time indices, this is more computationally costly than
> > > > if you build a bespoke model that allows different max-T for each j
> > > > (you can do this with rgeneric). However, the cost of AR(1)
> > > > computations is only of order linear in T, so whether it's worth the
> > > > extra implementation effort depends on how "imbalanced" your T-values
> > > > are.
> > > >
> > > > I'm not sure if this answers your question...

messages.body_plain:
Observing one x will have an effect on all the x values for that individual, so two observations for one individual will have a joint effect on the entire time series for that individual.

On Fri, 19 Aug 2022, 19:30 JJ Hubbard, <jordanj...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks Finn, that does help explain a lot. So in $summary.random I have all of the distributions for my X_t,j and the model constructs X_t,j even when time timestep t does not exist for individual j. But these won't be present in the *.fitted.values since there isn't actually an observation for them.
> Does the fitting of an observation x_{t_i,j_i} have any effect on the fitting of a different observation x_{t_k,j_k} where k != i? My coworkers and I have been discussing whether adding a new term will affect the posterior distributions of other terms.
>
> On Friday, August 19, 2022 at 9:08:57 AM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > this is more a question of what the Baeysian methodology does rather
> > than any particular thing about how INLA does prediction; it just does
> > the best it can at computing information about the posterior
> > distributions for the specified model.
> >
> > It doesn't reconstruct a "0th" observation. It just reconstructs all
> > the latent variables of the defined model.
> > Consider the case when the specified model has iid replicates of a
> > time-stationary AR(1) process model, and the observation model is
> > additive Gaussian noise, and the only other model component is an
> > intercept.
> > Let the AR(1) variables be x_{t,j}, for time t and individual j, with
> > variance \sigma_x^2 and AR correlation parameter \rho.
> >
> > Then for observation i, the linear predictor evaluates that for some
> > time t_i and individual j_i:
> > \eta_i = x_{t_i,j_i} + \beta_0
> > The observed values are
> > y_i = \eta_i + \eps_i,
> > where \eps_i ~ N(0,\sigma_e^2).
> >
> > The *.fitted.values output contains the posterior distribution
> > information for the \eta_i values. (i.e. the sum of \beta_0 and
> > x-values for observed times&individuals)
> > The *.random output contains the posterior distribution information
> > for the x_{t,j} values.
> >
> > The x-variables exist regardless of the observations. The f()
> > mechanism allows us to construct models where x_{t,j} is defined on
> > the full grid of all combinations of t=1,...,T and j=1,...,J,
> > and the summary.random output will contain the posterior distribution
> > information for all of those variables, regardless of whether some or
> > all have been observed.
> > If you plot the posterior std.dev <http://std.dev> values for all t=1,...,T for a
> > single individual, you should see small values for times associated
> > with observations, and progressively larger values for further,
> > unobserved, time points.
> > If the covariance parameters were known and fixed, the variances for
> > observed time points would be on the order of
> > 1 / (1 / \sigma_x^2 + 1 / \sigma_e^2)
> > (not exactly that, but as a rough guide) and then increasing towards
> > \sigma_x^2 the further from the observed time points you get.
> > For an individual that hasn't been observed at all,
> >
> > For cases where for some individuals you only have observations for
> > the first few time indices, this is more computationally costly than
> > if you build a bespoke model that allows different max-T for each j
> > (you can do this with rgeneric). However, the cost of AR(1)
> > computations is only of order linear in T, so whether it's worth the
> > extra implementation effort depends on how "imbalanced" your T-values
> > are.
> >
> > I'm not sure if this answers your question...
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > On Fri, 19 Aug 2022 at 16:18, JJ Hubbard <jordanj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > When looking at model$summary.hyperpar the mean SD for my observations is on the order of 10^-2. For PACF1 it is ~.9
> > >
> > > Could you explain more about INLA's process for reconstructing/predicting the observations that are not recorded for some participants? You explained how for an individual's first observation, INLA will try to reconstruct a 0th observation for the 1st observation's lag.
> > >
> > > I was surprised to find when looking at model$summary.random that the matrix had max_num_observations * num_individuals rows. Some of my participants might have 3 observations, others 30, so in this case INLA would reconstruct/predict these 27 observations that don't exist right?
> > >
> > > Does this have any impact on accuracy of my model? If it cannot reconstruct them well, could it bring performance down? I am wondering if my use case would be better with a custom method via 'rgeneric' like you mentioned, since the data is so unbalanced.

> > >>
> > >> And the corresponding sd values? If the observation noise variance is estimated to be small, then the AR estimates will pass vary close to the observed values with small posterior sd. > > >>> The AR model is defined to be stationary, i.e. at time 1 it has the

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

In model estimated with INLA with more than one likelihood (say, using multiple stacks, e.g., 'gaussian' and 'poisson'), we are given just one posterior marginal log-likelihood number in the output. Would it be possible to disentangle this with respect to the different types of responses in the stack corresponding to the different types of likelihood?

I hope this question makes sense.

Thanks,
Jon

messages.subject_clean: CARbayesST models in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I was originally using the models in package  CARbayesST for spatiotemporal modeling, but due to MCMC convergence issues, I started trying INLA. I'm having some difficulty when implementing the models in package  CARbayesST using INLA, and I can't get
enough help by searching Google, so I'm here to ask for help.

The first question, I think the Leroux-AR1 model will fit my data well, so I try to describe this model with the following code in inla, but when I apply this INLA model on the example used in the tutorial of the CARbayesST package, the result I get is far different from the MCMC results.
Random effect (from CARbayesST vignette):

formula: f(idarea, model = 'besagproper2', graph = W, group = idtime, control.group=list(model='ar1')

For the second question, I also tried to use the ANOVA model in INLA. The model formula and code are as follows. On the same sample data, the coefficients of the fixed effects of this result are very close to the MCMC results as I expected, but there is a clear difference in WAIC.
Random effect (from CARbayesST vignette):
formula:  f(idtime, model = "besagproper2", graph = D) + f(idarea, model = "besagproper2", graph = W) + f(id, model = "iid")

I'm unsure if these problems are caused by my wrong INLA formula or something else. Can anyone give me some clues?

Thank you very much.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Inla implements ar(1) as a stationary model, I.e. the marginal variance is constant. The way eq(5) from the other package is written, it looks as if they instead treat the model as having the initial variance equal to the subsequent conditional variances. That is equivalent to having an imagined phi_0 = 0 initial condition instead of a stationary model. If that’s really what they implemented, that might explain differences. Check if the estimated phi values for the first time point seem to be larger (in absolute value) for inla than for the other package.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I create indices like so:

df = df %>% group_by(ID) %>% mutate(index = rank(date_f))

The result is an individual's first observation is given by index == 1 and they increment by 1 every observation. Residuals are just `model$summary.fitted.values$mean - df$target`. One interesting thing is that changing the prior seems to alleviate the issue.

The questionable prior is `hyper_fixed = list(theta1=list(initial=0.5, fixed=T))` while `hyper_AR_f  = list(theta1 = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(3 * target_ln_sd, 0.01)), theta2 = list(prior="pc.cor1", param=c(0.9, 0.9)))`

messages.body_plain:
Hi
I have a model like
n <- 5380
ID <- seq(1:n)

r1 <- inla(respvar ~ -1 + Intercept + expvar1 + expvar2 + expvar3 + f(ID, model = 'iid') + f(w, model = open_spde,
data = inla.stack.data(mystack),
control.compute = control.compute = list(dic = T, waic = T, cpo = T),
control.predictor = list(compute = T, A = inla.stack.A(mystack))

Now I want to evaluate the effect of the fixed effects and the random effects individually on the values predicted by the model. In traditional mixed effects models you'd call this the marginal and conditional R-squared, i.e. how much does the random effects and the fixed effects contribute to the model respectively. I believe (and have tried without luck) that this maybe can be achieved with linear combinations, but could someone please direct me in a direction? Ideally with some example code, that shows how to enter the random effects into make.lincombs if that is the way to go. Maybe there is no good solution to this problem?

messages.subject: Spatio-temporal hurdle model with areal data in INLA
messages.subject_clean: Spatio-temporal hurdle model with areal data in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA Maintainers,

I am attempting to model similar data to that used in the Parana rainfall example in the Krainski et al. 2021 book, Section 8.5, i.e. a hurdle model that predicts the presence of a response and then the magnitude of response across space and time. However, my data are irregular lattice data (county borders), rather than points, and have an associated spatial weights matrix. I am wondering if these kind of data can be analyzed as a two-likelihood model, but without using the mesh. In particular, the inla.stack() command seems to imply A derived from something like inla.spde.make.A().

Any help in using the inla.stack() command with areal data would be much appreciated. Please let me know if you have any questions.

Best,
Dan

messages.body_plain:
I have specified this AR model with some fixed and random effects:

m1 <- inla(Y~ -1
    + FixedEffect1

    + RandomEffect1

    + f(observation_number, model='ar1',
        replicate=ID,
        values=1:max(df2$ observation_number  ),
        hyper=hyper_AR,
        constr=FALSE
    )

    , data=df2, family="gaussian"
    , control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive",  int.strategy="auto")
    , control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE, dic=TRUE, config=TRUE)
    , control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(1/0.01^2))), fixed=TRUE)
    , verbose=TRUE
    )

My coworkers and I are confused as to what value the AR1 term is lagging on. I am assuming that it is lagging on the response variable like in any typical AR definition

Y_t = sum i from 1 to n of rho_i * Y_t-i + epsilon_t

so my AR1 should be Y_t = rho * Y_t-1 + epsilon_t

Some think that the AR term is lagging on the random effects, and not the response variable.

Thank you

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] What is the math behind INLA's AR model?
messages.body_plain:
So that doc gives this:
x1 ∼ N (0,(τ (1 − ρ 2 ))−1 )
x_i = ρ * x_i−1 + epsilon_i ; epsilon_i ∼ N (0, τ −1 ) i = 2, . . . , n

Which does not depend on any variable from the data since x1 is just a draw from this normal distribution and all future x_1+t values are just multiples of x_t and a learned parameter plus noise. What effect does this try to capture? An AR1 is intuitive to me: I believe that my process at time t is a product of the process value at time t-1 with some parameter to be learned, plus an error term. The specification in INLA does not depend on my Y, nor does it depend on any predictive variable in X, so is it just to account for the error from the individual's previous observation?

messages.body_plain:
The ...eval function is a little special, as it assign simulated values
to each component in the  model automatically. like if

y ~ x + f(z, model="...")

then

inla.posterior.sample.eval(
	function() {
		## here 'x' will be the regression coefficient

		## while 'z' will be the vector defined by f(z, ..)

		## so if we want the Predictor (which is also
		## an automatic variable) then we need to
		## pass the covariates 'x', but now 'x' means
		## the regression coefficent, so that require
		## a small fix...
	})

like

fun = function (x.cov) { return (Intercept + x * xx.cov + z) }

and then pass x.cov in the args

inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, samples, x.cox=data$x)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Finn,

I have a few quick queries related to this discussion so will reply here rather than starting another thread.

I have the same motivation as the OP - to include a temporally (and spatially) varying covariate within a spatio-temporal inlabru model. It seems there are 2 ways to do this - either by defining a function fun(x,y,year) as the OP has done, or through using the built in component arguments (main_layer/main_selector). I'm a little unclear on both of these.

Function approach - are there any spatio-temporal examples for how to do this for standard data types? The function used by the OP may work well, but unsure of the format of certain objects i.e. 'year2', so it isn't helpful in understanding how an f(x,y,time) function should be constructed.

Component arguments - from this thread it seems like this may be more straightforward/reliable for standard gridded data formats anyway, i.e. SpatialGridDataFrame. However I'm not sure what the difference is between the main_layer and main_selector arguments, and which formats are considered "standard" for these to work. From the Reference manual it is not clear to me, apologies. There are also layer and selector arguments within the bru_fill_missing function and I'm not sure how to interpret these either, presumably they operate in a very similar way.

E.g. Say you have a SpatialGridDataFrame containing 3 covariate data layers with arbitrary names - one for each discrete time step - you wish to include within your model (covarSGDF). You also have a SpatialPointsDataFrame containing data observations in each of the 3 time steps that we wish to model, with a column "year" containing a numeric index (1-3) of which each time step the observations correspond to. Would either of the following be the correct argument usage? If not, how should the data format / arguments be changed. Should "year" be a separate index vector?

covar(main = covarSGDF, main_selector = "year", model = "linear") or
covar(main = covarSGDF, main_layer = "year", model = "linear")

Any further information on exactly how the layer and selector are working would be massively appreciated!

Best wishes,
Charles

messages.body_plain:
Hi Charles,

there are too many potential data storage formats for space-time data
to give clear answers for the general case; the function method leaves
the data extraction details to the user who hopefully knows their data
best.
The first of the two versions with SpatialGrid DataFrame below is how
it was supposed to work, but I think I made a logic mistake when
implementing it. More comments below.

> E.g. Say you have a SpatialGridDataFrame containing 3 covariate data layers with arbitrary names - one for each discrete time step - you wish to include within your model (covarSGDF). You also have SpatialPointsDataFrame containing data observations in each of the 3 time steps that we wish to model, with a column "year" containing a numeric index (1-3) of which each time step the observations correspond to. Would either of the following be the correct argument usage? If not, how should the data format / arguments be changed. Should "year" be a separate index vector?

covar(main = covarSGDF, main_selector = "year", model = "linear") or

If I read the inlabru code correctly, it tries to find the selector in
the covarSGDF object, but that doesn't really make sense. It would
make more sense for it to pick the 1,2,3 year information from the
general data object, so it can get a different year value for each
observation. I'll need to fix that bug! In the meantime you'll need to
use the function method. See the utils.R code in inlabru, function
eval_SpatialDF for possible inspiration.

covar(main = covarSGDF, main_layer = "year", model = "linear")

THis would just extract the year information, so is not what you need.

Finn

On Wed, 2022-08-24 at 04:07 -0700, Jesper Erenskjold Moeslund wrote:
> Thanks a lot for this elaboration. Three questions arise.
> 1: I still do not understand the v.index in your example. Where does
> the function get this index from when you call v.index? Is ".index"
> some built-in function that does something I apparently cannot read
> anywhere I have searched? And shouldn't it be v.idx.index in any case?
> The code runs, so probably not, I just don't understand why.
>

it is just a 'naming' thing.

	f(i)

this can be interpreted as effect 'f' indexed by 'i', so

	f[i]

in vector/R notation, so that

y ~ 1 + x + f(i)

means

Predictor = Intercept + beta.x * x + f[i]

in the 'eval' function, then 'beta.x' is named 'x' (as usual in lm/glm),
whereas 'f' is named 'x', then we need

Predictor = Intercept + x * x.covariate + i[i.index]

where 'x.covariate' is the 'x-covariate', and 'i.index' is 'i' as above

so

fun = function(x.covariate, i.index)
	return (Intercept + x * x.covariate + i[i.index])

with

	...eval(..., x.covariate=x, i.index=i)

where 'x' and 'i' is in the formula above.

> 2: Is it correct that in the function, given the example above, you
> could write either:
>        function () { return (Intercept + Predictor + z) }
> or
>        function (xcov1, xcov2,...) { return (Intercept + x1 * xcov1 +
> x2 * xcov2 ... + z)}
> or is this totally misunderstood?

The 'Predictor' is the linear predictor, hence the sum of all terms in
the formula, so with

y ~ 1 + x + f(i)

the Predictor = Intercept + beta.x * x + f[i]

>
> 3: Why couldn't the function in the first and really nice example not
> be:
> function () { return c(Intercept + Predictor, Intercept + Predictor -
> v.idx) }
> >

'v.idx' is likely of a different length then 'Predictor' and/or the
index ordering is not the same, hence you need to index that one to get
it right.

Note that 'Intercept' is part of 'Predictor' hence not needed.

please try out with some small simple examples to make sure you get
understand it correct.

there should be a vignette about this, if anyone... please let me know

--

messages.subject: barrier model specification and interpretation
messages.subject_clean: barrier model specification and interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am working through a gamma hurdle model with a spatial barrier and wanted to ensure that my specification of the model and interpretation of the output was correct. My response in the model (gamma portion) is catch-per-effort and I have 2 categorical covariates, gear (2 levels; EF and DT) and habitat (3 levels; Trib, MC, and SC) in my model. I have created the model as follows:

# create the gamma response
SVC2$pos <- ifelse(SVC2$CPUE_Ped_Hr > 0, SVC2$CPUE_Ped_Hr, NA)

# create the model matrix
Xm <- model.matrix(~ fGear + fHabitat, data = SVC2)
X <- data.frame(fGearDT = Xm[, 2],
                fHabitatMC = Xm[, 3],
                fHabitatSC = Xm[, 4])

# create the stack including the spatial random field
stack.gamma9 <- inla.stack(tag = 'GammaFit9',
                           data = list(pos = SVC2$pos),
                           A = list(1, 1, 1, A2),
                           effects = list(Intercept = rep(1, N),
                                          X = X,
                                          Site = SVC2$Site,
                                          w = w2.index))

# write the formula
fgamma9 <- formula(pos ~ -1 + Intercept + fGearEF + fHabitatSC + fHabitatTrib +
                     f(Site, model = 'iid') + f(w, model = spde2))

# run the model
system.time(
barrier.g <- inla(fgamma9,
                  family = 'gamma',
                  data = inla.stack.data(stack.gamma9),
                  control.compute = list(dic = T,
                                         waic = T),
                  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack.gamma9),
                                           link = 1))
)

summary(barrier.g)

and get the folllowing output.

Fixed effects:
                    mean    sd  0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant   mode kld
Intercept     3.773 1.292      0.979    3.832      6.162  3.910   0
fGearEF      -0.906 0.122     -1.146   -0.907     -0.666 -0.907   0
fHabitatSC    0.381 0.215     -0.035    0.380      0.807  0.376   0
fHabitatTrib  0.724 0.417     -0.104    0.726      1.536  0.731   0

Random effects:
  Name      Model
    Site IID model
   w RGeneric2

Model hyperparameters:
                                                 mean     sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant   mode
Precision parameter for the Gamma observations   1.86  0.031       1.80     1.86       1.92   1.86
Precision for Site                             487.49 11.031     466.12   487.36     509.71 487.11
Theta1 for w                                    -1.25  0.109      -1.49    -1.23      -1.08  -1.17
Theta2 for w                                     5.65  0.022       5.61     5.65       5.69   5.64

Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) ...............: 1747.71
Deviance Information Criterion (DIC, saturated) ....: 3086.76
Effective number of parameters .....................: 18.98

Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) ...: 1750.69
Effective number of parameters .................: 18.76

Marginal log-Likelihood:  -916.40
 is computed
Posterior summaries for the linear predictor and the fitted values are computed
(Posterior marginals needs also 'control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)')

My questions are:
1) Is including the random effects of site (includes multiple sampling locations) and the spatial component in the same model valid, or will these random effects be confounded?

2) I am interpreting the fixed effects as indicating that there is a negative effect of gear = EF relative to gear = DT but the potential effects of habitat are unimportant (95% credible intervals overlap 0), but I'm not sure how to interpret the hyperparameters. I've been primarily using the Zuur et al. 2018 book (GAM and zero-inflated models) to guide my analysis and haven't found a concise explanation for the interpretation of these values. Guidance is appreciated.

3) Is there a way to understand the potential site or spatial effects on the gear differences? Essentially, this would be examining an interaction among gear and site/space to determine if the relationship among gears changes throughout the study area.

4) What is the interpretation of the spatial random field (obtained using barrier.g$summary.random$w$mean; figure attached axes are in UTM/1000) and is there a way to understand the magnitude of the differences? Based on my reading, I would interpret this as indicating that areas in red have relatively high catch-per-effort (regardless of gear) and areas in blue have relatively low catch-per effort but the magnitude of the differences is unclear.

5) Is there another book/resource that you would recommend as a guide? I have seen several on the R-INLA website but I'm not sure which might be most appropriate for understanding the interpretation of the output from this type of analysis.

I know that that is a lot of questions but I really appreciate any help or guidance.
Thanks,
Ben

messages.subject: Re: barrier model specification and interpretation
messages.subject_clean: barrier model specification and interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

(1) Having the random site effect plus the spatial field seems fine to me. You can think of the field as a spatially smoothed intercept and the random site effect as describing the local deviation around the field.
(2a) "negative effect of gear = EF relative to gear = DT"  That seems right to me.
(2b) "the potential effects of habitat are unimportant" That's what the contrasts suggest, but another way to test that is to run another model without any habitat effects and compare WAIC.
(2c) The hyperparameter summaries tell you how much variation is accounted for by the different model components. Variation is expressed as precision (1/variance). Precision for Gamma obs = 1.86 is another way of saying that the raw residual in the model has an SD of sqrt(1/1.86)) = 0.73. Precision for site = 488 is like saying the site effect has a SD of sqrt(1/488) = 0.05, which is small compared to raw residual (0.73). One of the theta1 and theta2 describes the variation explained by the spatial field and the other describes the range of the spatial decay function (where the spatial correlation coefficient decreases to around 0.1). I don't remember which is which. What are your spatial units? Meters? Kilometers? Not sure why theta1 is a negative number.
(3) There is a way to see if the gear effects vary across space. It is called a spatially varying coefficient model. The newest versions of INLA and inlabru have a vignette for how to build an SVC model.
(4) I think you have the interpretation of the field correct? The spatial field is a smooth adjustment to the global intercept, yes? As for magnitude, think about any transformations needed. Does the gamma model use a log link?
(5) There are several great references. In many cases the authors are kind enough to provide an accessible ebook. For example: https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ and https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/index.html.

Best,
Tim

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to define covariates with temporal variations in inlabru?

messages.body_plain:
Hi again Charles,

I've double checked the inlabru internals, and I was wrong about there
being a bug; the feature is actually implemented as intended!
What you need is this component specification:

  covar(main = covarSGDF, main_selector = "year", model = "linear")

For this to work, the data argument to like() must have include a
column/variable called "year", containing either numerical or
character value that can be used to index the layers/columns of
covarSGDF.

Finn

messages.subject: Interpreting ii2d random effects
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting ii2d random effects
messages.body_plain:
I need some help interpreting model random effects for an iid2d model

If I have 10 subjects, and want to fit a slope for each subject on two factors. Those slopes are correlated, so I'm using an iid2d mode.

The model fits, and the errors look OK.

However, when looking at the model$summary.random values, I get a list of TWO random effects. Each random effect has 20 rows.

My understanding is that there should be a vector of 2*n_subjects. (First 10 rows are effect 1, and second 10 rows are effect 2). However, the model is giving me two data.frames, EACH with 2*n_subjects.

How can I interpret this? i.e. for Subject 5, what is the mean of the random effect for the two effect?
(I would expect it to be row 5 and row 15. But, of WHICH summary.random?)

```
n_subject <- length(unique(d$subjects))

model <- inla(score ~ 1
+ f(subject_id, test_number, model="iid2d", n=2*n_subject, hyper=hyper_subject)
+ f(subject_id_2, test_number_2, copy="subject_id")
, data=d, family="gaussian"
, control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive", int.strategy="auto")
)
```

messages.subject: interpreting hyperparameters from a spatial gamma model
messages.subject_clean: interpreting hyperparameters from a spatial gamma model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am running a spatial gamma model and I'm having some trouble interpreting the hyperparameters from the model. The model formula is:

fgamma9 <- formula(pos ~ -1 + Intercept + fGearEF + fHabitatSC + fHabitatTrib +
                     f(Site, model = 'iid') + f(w, model = spde2))

and the output is:

Fixed effects:
                    mean    sd  0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant   mode kld
Intercept     3.773 1.292      0.979    3.832      6.162  3.910   0
fGearEF      -0.906 0.122     -1.146   -0.907     -0.666 -0.907   0
fHabitatSC    0.381 0.215     -0.035    0.380      0.807  0.376   0
fHabitatTrib  0.724 0.417     -0.104    0.726      1.536  0.731   0

Random effects:
  Name      Model
    Site IID model
   w RGeneric2

Model hyperparameters:
                                                 mean     sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant   mode
Precision parameter for the Gamma observations   1.86  0.031       1.80     1.86       1.92   1.86
Precision for Site                             487.49 11.031     466.12   487.36     509.71 487.11
Theta1 for w                                    -1.25  0.109      -1.49    -1.23      -1.08  -1.17
Theta2 for w                                     5.65  0.022       5.61     5.65       5.69   5.64

Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) ...............: 1747.71
Deviance Information Criterion (DIC, saturated) ....: 3086.76
Effective number of parameters .....................: 18.98

Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) ...: 1750.69
Effective number of parameters .................: 18.76

Marginal log-Likelihood:  -916.40
 is computed
Posterior summaries for the linear predictor and the fitted values are computed
(Posterior marginals needs also 'control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)')

I understand the precision for the gamma observations and the precision for site to be a measure of the variation attributable to the raw residuals and sites, respectively (thanks, Tim), but I'm not sure how to interpret theta1 and theta2. I've looked through various resources, but haven't found a concise explanation for these hyperparameters. Can anyone explain these to me or point me to a paper or book that defines them?
Thanks,
Ben

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] interpreting hyperparameters from a spatial gamma model
messages.body_plain:
The interpretation of theta1 and and theta2 depends on the spde parameterisation, which can be user defined. The default parameterisation is theta1=log(tau) and theta2=log(kappa) in the spde formulation.
However, I would recommend using the inla.spde2.pcmatern() model instead, since that uses a parameterisation that gives the correlation range and marginal standard deviation instead, which is more directly interpretable.

Finn

messages.subject: Do AR(1) Replicate models have a single rho?
messages.subject_clean: Do AR(1) Replicate models have a single rho?
messages.body_plain:
The INLA AR(1) doc gives:

x1 ∼ N (0,(τ (1 − ρ 2 ))−1 )
xi = ρ xi−1 + i ; i ∼ N (0, τ −1 ) i = 2, . . . , n

as the math for an AR model. Is there a single distribution for rho learned for all subjects in a replicate model? Or Does each subject get their own rho distribution that will be learned?

Also, is rho constant between time indices for an AR(1), or is there a unique distribution for rho between t=1 and t=2, and between t=3 and t=4?

Thank you very much
